title: Still Operational
revision: Draft 1.0 — The Broken Link (first full draft)
paragraphs: At four forty-eight in the morning, Andrew discovered that Darius had prepared enough food to survive a very small siege.
The evidence occupied the common-room table in eight paper-wrapped parcels. Darius stood beside them with a pencil and a look of concentration usually reserved for recipes he was inventing.
“You're not taking all of that into combat,” Andrew said.
“Of course not,” Darius replied. “Some of it is for the journey.”

Nico appeared in the doorway, fastening the collar of his uniform with one hand and holding a piece of toast with the other. His curls had been crushed on one side by a night's sleep and remained rebelliously upright on the other.
“Is there coffee?” Nico asked.
“Good morning to you too,” Andrew said.
Nico regarded him. “I didn't want to waste valuable time saying things we both already know.”
“There's coffee,” Darius said. “It's not good coffee.”
“You made it. I trust you.”
“I didn't make the coffee.”
Nico stopped chewing. “Ah.”

Mara came in with a folded route card and a mug that looked as if she'd been drinking from it for an hour. Her hair was tied back tightly. She had already changed into her flight uniform, and there were dry mud marks at the cuffs from yesterday's reconnaissance around the depot.
“Fuel reserves checked. Northern corridor still open,” Mara said. “The first road gate expects us at five twenty.”
“Morning, Mara,” Andrew said.
“Good morning. The road gate expects us at five twenty.”
“See? She understands priorities,” Nico said.

Mara unfolded the card and held it toward Andrew. “The local detour report came in at three. No changes near the relay, but a bridge north of Hamburg is closed to heavy traffic. We'll use the western bypass.”
Andrew studied the route. The change would cost them a few minutes, maybe more if the checkpoint was busy. He'd rather lose the minutes than discover that a damaged bridge couldn't hold eight XR-17s.
“Use the bypass,” he said.
Mara looked faintly disappointed.
“You wanted an argument?” Andrew asked.
“Not especially.”
“You've been awake too long if you're disappointed by agreement.”
“I've been awake exactly as long as necessary.”
“That's what I tell Yelena,” Andrew said.
“Which is how I know it's a lie,” Yelena said from the doorway.

The medic carried a small case in one hand and an open notebook in the other. Her ash-brown braid lay over her shoulder. She didn't appear to have slept either, but Andrew knew better than to ask. She could become impressively offended by questions she asked everyone else.
“Nico, how many hours?” she said.
“Of what?”
“Sleep.”
“Ah. We are discussing personal matters before breakfast.”
“Four?”
“Five,” Nico said.
“Four and a half,” Andrew corrected.
Nico turned on him. “Traitor.”
“That's better than yesterday,” Yelena said, making a note.
“You're recording our failures now?” Nico asked.
“Only the ones with names.”
Juno arrived last, carrying a spanner he'd apparently forgotten to put down. The knuckles of his right hand were still marked with old grease. He spotted the breakfast parcels and picked one up.
“Is this mine?”
“Yes,” Darius said.
“Brilliant.”
“Did you sleep in the hangar again?” Mara asked.
“No, mate. I visited the hangar before coming here.”
“Your room is on the other side of the building,” Andrew said.
“Exactly. Had to make a proper trip of it.”
“Juno.”

“The bearing's perfect,” Juno said, anticipating the question. “Checked the housing, checked the grease, checked the travel. Nothing's shifted since yesterday. I'll run another diagnostic once the reactor's warm.”
“You already signed it off.”
“Yeah. And now I'm checking it again. That's the thing about repairs. You can be right twice.”
Sera entered quietly behind him and set her tablet on the table.
“You didn't check the left-rear thermal coupling,” she said.
Juno glanced back. “I did.”
“Three days ago.”
“Still counts.”
“Not for a two-hundred-kilometer drive.”
Juno stared at her for a moment. Then he picked up his parcel and sighed.
“Fine. I will check it again.”
Sera nodded. “Thank you.”
It occurred to Andrew that Sera could make Juno behave faster than any disciplinary action he'd ever tried. She rarely raised her voice and almost never wasted a word.
Akari pushed into the room with her camera hanging against her chest.
“Everybody,” she announced, “I have something important.”
“No,” Mara said.
“You haven't heard it yet.”
“I know.”
Akari turned to Andrew. “Can I get a picture at the gate? Just the mechs leaving together. It would look amazing if you all lined up properly.”
“We're not delaying a military operation for a photograph,” Andrew said.
“I only need ten seconds.”
Nico made a noise of outrage. “You said that yesterday.”
“Yesterday you moved!”
“Because you stepped on my foot!”
“I did not.”
“You nearly did,” Mara said.
Akari pointed at her. “You see? No actual injury. Perfectly safe.”
Andrew took one of the breakfast parcels and slipped it into his jacket. “Get a picture from the courtyard if you can do it without holding anyone up.”
Akari smiled immediately. “You are an excellent commander.”
“That's an opinion you can put in the report.”
She was already on her way to the door.

Darius watched her go, then passed the remaining food around. The little parcels contained bread rolls with cheese and something sweet that Andrew couldn't identify. Darius had written names on the wrappers, though Nico was already trying to negotiate a trade.
“Mine has the best one,” Nico told Juno.
“You haven't opened yours,” Juno replied.
“I can tell.”
“Then keep it.”
Nico frowned. “You're very difficult this morning.”

A few minutes later they crossed the courtyard, boots splashing through last night's rainwater. The converted depot looked almost sleepy beneath the low clouds: a kitchen window glowing yellow, the old administration wing, the patched hangar roof, a pair of utility trucks by the gate. It was hard to believe that eight combat mechs could live here without making the whole place seem more military than it did.
Then the hangar doors opened.

The XR-17s waited in two rows, their armored bodies crouched low between six articulated legs. Turrets faced the central aisle. The narrow, aggressive cockpits were dark until their pilots approached and the boarding systems woke in sequence.
Juno stopped beside his mech and ran his palm over the repaired front joint.
“Morning, sweetheart,” he murmured.
Nico heard him. “You talk to it like it's your girlfriend.”
“She's less argumentative than you.”
“It's because she can't answer.”
A maintenance display lit on the side of Juno's chassis. Sera looked at it, then at him.
“Left-rear thermal coupling.”
“Yep. Doing it now.”

Andrew headed for his own cockpit. The boarding ladder dropped from beneath the hull, and he climbed into the narrow compartment, pulled the harness across his shoulders and settled his boots onto the control rests.

His displays came alive in a familiar sequence. Reactor temperature. Joint alignment. Weapon safeties. Eight friendly identification markers appeared in the yard as the other pilots brought their systems online.
“Andrew to all units,” he said into the squad channel. “Radio check.”
“Mara. Clear.”
“Darius. Clear.”
“Juno. Clear, mate.”
“Akari. Perfectly clear.”
“Sera. Clear.”
“Yelena. Clear.”
“Nico. Testing. One, two, three. The handsome young communications officer wishes everyone a pleasant journey.”
“Nico,” Mara said, “clear your channel.”
“Technically it was already clear.”
Andrew suppressed a smile. Eight markers. Eight voices. Everyone here.

“Weapons safe through the civilian corridor,” he said. “Mara leads the route. Keep your spacing around settlements, and nobody passes a checkpoint without clearance. We'll meet the repair team at the northern depot.”
“Understood,” Mara said.

Andrew shifted the controls. His XR-17 lifted from its resting posture, all six legs extending together until the cockpit rose above the hangar floor. He felt the weight transfer through the chassis, the faint vibration as the reactor took the load.
Outside, Akari's cockpit canopy was still open. She had her camera raised.
“Hold still!” she shouted over the common channel.
“We're leaving,” Mara said.
“I'm taking it now.”
The eight mechs were halfway through arranging themselves into a column when Akari's camera clicked. It would be another terrible picture. Andrew hoped she kept it.
The depot gate slid aside.
“Move out,” Andrew said.
The column stepped through, turned north, and accelerated.

At first the mechs moved with the careful precision required by the roads near Celle. Their clawed feet landed on the paved shoulders beside the military lane, each step measured to avoid broken drainage covers and civilian cables. The six-legged gait was almost gentle at this speed. The pilots could have been escorting a parade.
The houses fell behind them.

Beyond the last checkpoint, the land opened into broad fields, low industrial buildings and service roads marked for military traffic. Mara took them onto a hardened strip running along the edge of an abandoned freight route.
“All units,” she said, “open section begins in two hundred meters. Maintain formation.”
The speed indicator climbed.

Andrew felt the XR-17 lengthen its stride. Its front legs reached forward, found ground and released almost before he registered the contact. The middle pair carried the weight through the turn of the gait; the rear pair drove the body onward. At speed, the movement became fluid enough that the cockpit scarcely pitched.
Forty miles an hour. Sixty. Eighty.
Juno's laughter came over the squad channel.
“That's more like it.”
“Save your enthusiasm for the inspection,” Sera said.
“I'm enthusiastic about that too.”

Andrew watched the speed touch ninety-seven, then settle. The XR-17s could sustain a hundred on open, favorable ground. Here the formation chose a little less to keep an easy margin between machines and preserve room to maneuver.
The fields passed in long, green-brown strips. A flock of birds lifted from a ditch, and Akari's mech shifted sideways to avoid the uneven ground. She did it without losing her place in line.
“That was a lovely turn,” Juno said.
“Thank you,” Akari replied. “You may compliment me again after the mission.”
“Didn't mean you. Meant the leg system.”
“You're impossible.”
“Put it in the report,” Juno said.

They slowed before the first occupied village. A faded school sign stood beside a row of houses with patched windows. On the square, traders had arranged jars, vegetables and homemade soap beneath an awning. A line of people waited outside a ration office. The eight XR-17s passed at a crawl.
A boy in a yellow coat waved both arms.
Akari raised her mech's right foreleg briefly.
“Akari,” Mara said, “watch your clearance.”
“Plenty of clearance.”
“The market stall disagrees.”
Akari lowered the leg. The boy laughed and kept waving.
Andrew saw a woman take the child's hand and pull him farther from the road. She didn't look angry. She just looked as if she'd already spent the morning being worried about other things.

At the next checkpoint, a column of civilian vehicles was waiting under a temporary roof of camouflage netting. Some had luggage tied to their roofs. Others carried mattresses, bicycles or plants in plastic buckets.
An elderly man sat on the edge of a truck bed, holding a cage covered with a towel. Whatever lived inside shifted when the XR-17s passed.
The checkpoint officer appeared on Andrew's forward display, helmet camera catching a tired face and a sleepless pair of eyes.
“Walker detachment?” the officer asked.
“That's us,” Andrew said. “Eight mechs, northbound to the Neumünster relay.”
“Your passage is cleared. Keep west after the next junction. Bridge crew's still working the eastern span.”
“Any changes up ahead?”
“Not on your assigned corridor. There's artillery farther north. Listen to the route channel if you want the depressing details.”
Andrew hesitated. “And the civilians?”
The officer glanced away from the camera. “Those who can go south are going south. Still got people coming north for work, if you can believe it.”
Andrew could.
The officer stepped aside, and the barrier lifted.

When the squad was clear, Mara switched them back to the military corridor. They accelerated again, though not as fast as before. A maintenance convoy occupied one lane, and beyond it crews were reinforcing a line of concrete barriers. Their bulldozer had lost a track and stood crooked beside the road.
Darius broke the quiet on the channel.
“Those people at the checkpoint have been waiting since before dawn,” he said.
“Probably longer,” Yelena replied.
“Do you think the old man had a cat?”
“In the cage?” Nico asked.
“It moved.”
“Could be a chicken,” Juno said.
“Not if Yelena has anything to say about it,” Akari replied.
Yelena paused. “A chicken is also a patient.”
Andrew smiled. The squad could find its way back to ordinary conversation almost anywhere. He wasn't sure whether it was a skill they'd learned or a habit they refused to give up.

North of Hamburg, the clouds lowered and the landscape changed. Defensive markers appeared beside the road, then concrete firing positions, then embankments built from earth and broken stone. The population was thinner here, though no less busy. Mechanics worked beneath vehicles. Uniformed volunteers carried cable drums. A group of children helped stack empty crates outside a clinic while a tired teacher tried to keep them away from the road.
On a rise to the east, Andrew could see an artillery battery adjusting its barrels.
The radio carried a request for replacement ammunition, followed by a reply too faint to make out.
“That's not our sector,” Mara said.
“I know,” Andrew replied.
A few moments later the ground gave a distant, hollow thud. The artillery line had fired.
Nico reduced the volume of the general traffic channel. “They've been busy.”
“Keep the local channel up,” Andrew said.
“Already is.”

Andrew checked the time. They'd covered most of the distance in a little over two hours, with the delays and slower sections accounting for as much of the journey as the open ground. Mara's estimate had been good.
The forward depot came into view shortly after eight.

It occupied the grounds of a former distribution center, surrounded by hurriedly built walls and an assortment of buildings that had not been designed to withstand a battle. One warehouse had lost half its roof. Workers had enclosed the loading docks with sandbags. A row of civilian vans waited behind concrete barriers.
There were fewer mechs here than Andrew expected.

The depot sentry cleared the gate for their eight XR-17s, then directed them to a hardened inspection pad. Andrew brought his mech down into a low waiting posture while the other seven took positions around the square.
“Don't block the medical entrance,” Mara said.
“Wasn't going to,” Nico replied.
“You're standing across it.”
“Ah.”
Nico shuffled his mech three meters to the side.

Andrew opened his canopy. Cool air washed across his face, carrying the smell of damp concrete and engine exhaust. He climbed down and found a woman in a faded orange work jacket waiting beneath the pad lights.
“Andrew Walker?” she asked.
“Yes.”
“Leonie Krüger. Communications maintenance.” She held out a gloved hand. “You're early.”
“We tried.”
“Good. I don't think this station has another afternoon to spare.”
Behind her, two small utility vans stood packed with replacement cable, tools and portable batteries. A young technician was checking a coil of wire, while an older driver studied a greasy map.
Leonie followed Andrew's glance. “That's Mika with the spare modules. Oskar drives the second van. Three technicians, two vans. We'd have come with half that if I thought I could get away with it.”
“What's failed?” Andrew asked.

“That depends on which piece of the relay you ask. The primary line started dropping packets two days ago. Last night the backup power feed became intermittent. We think water got into a coupling housing during the storm.”
“You think?” Mara asked as she climbed down from her own cockpit.
Leonie gave her a look. “If it were certain, I'd be standing at the relay with a replacement part instead of standing here explaining why we need an escort.”
Mara nodded. “Fair.”

A thin man in a stained field jacket emerged from the depot office. His sleeve carried a worn service insignia. He introduced himself as Sergeant Brandt and brought them inside to a map pinned over a table.

“Relay's here,” Brandt said, tapping a mark northeast of the depot. “The eastern bridge is underwater. Engineers closed it last night. West route goes through the old workshop ground and cuts back toward the relay after the drainage culvert.”
“Mara's route,” Andrew said.
Brandt looked at her. “Good choice. We used it for recovery traffic before the floods.”
“West watch?” Mara asked.
“Two observation posts, intermittent contact. One crew pulled back before dawn to support the northern batteries.”
“Which one?” Andrew asked.
Brandt pointed to the post overlooking the road's far side.
Andrew studied the map. That post would have watched the blind section.
“We requested coverage,” Mara said.
“Request reached us,” Brandt replied. “We can't give you people we don't have.”
He didn't offer a dramatic explanation. He simply moved his finger north.

“Two sectors have been asking for reinforcements since midnight. We're still holding here. My job is to make certain your technicians get through. Yours is to make certain the road stays open long enough to do it.”
Leonie leaned over the map. “And my job is to fix the relay before another convoy spends a night parked in the open.”
“Exactly,” Andrew said.

He asked Brandt for the latest patrol times. Mara compared them with the water report. Nico checked their short-range channels and arranged a backup set of coded light signals in case the local radios failed. Sera pulled up the forward observation feeds. Juno inspected the repaired joint on his own mech and checked the heat readings, ignoring Nico's commentary while he worked.
Yelena opened Leonie's medical case.
“You have dressings,” Yelena said.
“Yes.”
“Tourniquets?”
Leonie pointed to a side pocket.
“Good. Keep them where you can reach them.”
Mika, the young technician, watched her repack the case.
“Will we need those?” he asked.
“Hopefully not,” Yelena said.
He didn't look reassured.
She closed the case and handed it back. “That's why we're bringing them.”
Andrew returned to the map. The western route was marked in pencil, with the old workshop yard circled in blue.

“Here's the hardstand,” Mara said. “If anything goes wrong, the vans stop here. The culvert's three hundred meters of poor sightline. We keep the mechs on both sides of the road as far as the ground allows.”
“Can your machines move faster than ours?” Leonie asked.
“A little,” Juno said from the door.
“Don't,” Sera said without looking up.
Leonie raised an eyebrow.
“A hundred miles an hour on good ground,” Andrew explained. “We won't be doing anything close to that near your vans.”
“Wonderful,” Leonie said. “I had enough reasons to be nervous.”
Andrew smiled. “We'll keep you together.”
Brandt's desk radio crackled. A voice from a northern battery requested confirmation of a firing lane. Brandt answered in clipped German, then switched the set off again.
“Stay on your assigned route,” he told Andrew. “I can't spare another unit if you go looking for a bigger fight.”
“We aren't looking for one.”
Brandt glanced at the eight mechs outside. “Glad to hear it.”
Andrew signed the escort sheet, passed the final route confirmation to Mara and climbed back into his XR-17.
“Everyone ready?” he asked on the squad channel.
One by one, seven voices answered.
The two utility vans started their engines. Their brake lights glowed red against the wet loading docks.
“Escort formation,” Andrew said. “Let's go put the north back on the radio.”
The two utility vans looked very small between eight XR-17s.

Andrew had seen columns like this before. A few ordinary vehicles carrying something essential, surrounded by mechs worth more than the roads beneath them. The people doing the essential work were rarely the ones with armor.
“Is this your normal escort speed?” Leonie asked over the local channel.
“Only when we're trying to impress people,” Nico said.
“Then I'm impressed.”
Nico sounded pleased. “At last. An appreciative audience.”
They were moving at barely thirty kilometers an hour. Andrew's mech placed its six feet carefully along the service road, its reactor barely working compared with the drive north.

Andrew and Mara led. Darius and Juno kept to either side of the vans. Sera monitored the eastern drainage channel, Akari screened the western fields, Nico handled communications, and Yelena covered the road behind them.

The road narrowed between fields heavy with rainwater. Ahead, the old eastern crossing had vanished beneath brown floodwater. Only the tops of two markers and the broken edge of the bridge were visible.
Mara indicated the submerged road on their shared display.
“Still want the direct route?” she asked.
“Not particularly,” Andrew said.
“Good.”
“Are you going to keep bringing this up?”
“Yes.”
The convoy turned west onto her service road.

It passed an abandoned workshop complex built around a broad paved yard. Most of the windows had been boarded over. A sign marked VEHICLE MAINTENANCE leaned against a fence. Someone had drawn a line through the word VEHICLE.
“Juno would like this place,” Nico said.
“Wouldn't mind a look,” Juno admitted.
“After the mission,” Andrew told him.
“That's what I was going to say.”
“No, it wasn't,” Sera replied.

Beyond the workshop yard, the service road curved toward the culvert. The drainage bank blocked the view beyond it for nearly three hundred meters. On Andrew's display, the far side remained an empty strip marked UNOBSERVED.
“Akari, any movement?” he asked.
“Nothing I can identify. But the east bank has fresh soil on it. Something climbed out of there recently.”
Sera checked her sensors. “Cold returns under the drainage channel. Most could be debris. Can't distinguish anything behind the concrete.”
“West watch?” Andrew asked.
Nico switched channels. “West watch, Walker escort approaching Culvert Three. Request visual on the northern exit.”
Static answered him.
He tried again.
“...watch two...” a distant voice said. “...east bank... movement...”
The signal failed.
“West watch, repeat your last,” Nico called.
Nothing.
Mara highlighted the paved workshop yard. “We hold the vans there. Two mechs forward, two protecting their retreat. Nobody enters the blind stretch until Akari clears it.”
“Agreed,” Andrew said. “Leonie, pull onto the hardstand and wait for our signal.”
“Understood.”
The first van turned through the workshop gate.
Akari climbed the small rise west of the road. Her mech remained low, turret facing the drainage embankment.
“Andrew,” she said, suddenly serious. “Movement. Eastern ditch.”
“How many?”
“More than I can count in one look.”
A figure rose behind the concrete edge of the culvert.

For an instant Andrew thought he was seeing a wounded civilian. It had two arms, two legs, a head with short dark hair and a pale, almost untouched face. The body emerged slowly, leaning forward as though exhausted.
Then both arms straightened together.

The figure lifted itself into a posture too balanced for a living person. Under its torn clothing, two identical lengths of metal ran down its chest. The machinery disappeared into flesh at the shoulders and emerged again beneath its ribs.
Another head appeared beside it.
Then a third.
“Huskframes,” Akari reported. “At least fifteen. More behind them.”
“Leonie, stop at the hardstand,” Andrew ordered. “Engines off. Stay in the vans.”
The first Huskframe dropped onto the road.
It staggered for two steps, corrected its footing with mechanical precision and ran straight toward the workshops.
Andrew's rotary cannon fired a short burst. The rounds struck the creature in the chest and knocked it backward into the ditch.
More Reclaimed came over the bank.

Their limbs mirrored one another perfectly. The human faces were not masks. He could see the pores of pale skin and the wet strands of hair, the familiar shapes of noses and cheeks. One wore the remains of a civilian jacket with a missing sleeve. The arm beneath it was built exactly like the uncovered one.
Two of them ran with their heads tipped to the same angle.
“Mara, take the left approach,” Andrew said. “Sera, suppress the ditch. Darius, Juno, guard those vans. Nobody chases a target away from the road.”
“Copy,” Mara answered.
Sera's rotary cannon opened up. Several Huskframes fell, but those behind them stepped into the gaps without pausing.
The sound of impacts beneath the road made Andrew check his footing.
A chunk of concrete lifted beside the culvert.
“Below us,” Sera warned.

A low body forced its way through the broken drainage opening. Four legs unfolded in mirrored pairs around a flat central torso. A human head hung beneath it, facing forward, its eyes half-open. The mouth moved as the creature began to run.
“Crawler!” Nico called.
It lunged at Andrew's front joint. He lifted the leg, moved sideways and fired downward, driving the Crawler into the open trench.
Another emerged behind it.
Then another.
The repair vans sat less than a hundred meters behind the squad's forward positions.
Darius turned his XR-17 sideways across the workshop entrance. Its six legs braced along the road edge, armored body protecting the vehicles while its turret tracked the drainage gap.
“Crawlers coming through the gate,” Nico warned.
“I see them,” Darius said.
One slipped beneath a fallen panel and reached the second van. Oskar shouted over the escort channel.
“Something's under us!”
“Don't move,” Yelena ordered.

She advanced from the rear, lowering her mech close enough to hook a foreleg beneath the creature without touching the van. The Crawler released the axle and grabbed for her joint. Yelena swung it into the empty trench and fired before it could climb out.
“Clear,” she said.
Oskar didn't answer at once.
“You can breathe now,” Yelena added.
A shaky laugh came over the radio.
At the northern edge of the workshops, a tall shape leaped over a broken wall.
It landed on both feet, long legs folding beneath a narrow torso. Its arms were equally long, matching at every joint, and its head remained perfectly upright while the rest of the body moved.
“Stalker, west side!” Akari called.
Juno turned toward it. His rotary cannon barked, but the creature changed direction between bursts and darted behind a workshop building.
“That's quick,” he said.
“Keep it away from the vans,” Andrew replied.
“On it.”

The Stalker came out of cover on Juno's right. He shifted his mech sharply, the repaired front bearing taking the strain without hesitation. The creature's claws scraped across an outer plate instead of reaching the joint. Juno fired at close range and caught its torso as it tried to spring away.
The Stalker collapsed against the wall, then reached forward once more before going still.
“Bearing's holding,” Juno reported.
“Good,” Sera said. “Focus on the other one.”
“Other one?”
“Behind Yelena.”
Akari was already moving.
Her mech swept around the workshop yard, six legs placing themselves in rapid succession over the broken ground. The second Stalker dropped from an embankment, aiming for the rear of Yelena's XR-17.
Akari fired as it landed.
The first burst struck the wall. The Stalker folded its limbs and tried to slip beneath the line of fire. Akari corrected and hit it before it could reach the road.
“Rear clear,” she said.
“Thank you,” Yelena replied.
“Now you owe me a favor.”
“You have a very short memory.”
“Several favors, then.”
For a moment, Andrew thought they had contained the attack.
The Huskframes at the culvert were thinning. Sera had the eastern bank covered, Mara held the west approach, and Darius remained between the technicians and anything that could reach them.
Then the remaining Huskframes changed direction.
They withdrew from the road, spreading to either side of the northern exit.
Something struck the culvert wall from beyond the embankment.
The concrete cracked.
A second impact tore away a slab the size of a small car.
Mara's voice came across the channel. “Andrew. Heavy contact.”
The Brute pushed through the opening.

Its torso rose above the road barriers, built from immense paired arms and legs around a broad armored chest. Under the armor, flesh and cables flexed together. Every major joint had an identical counterpart, each limb balanced against the other with awful precision.
At the center of its upper body was an intact human head.

The man had neatly parted dark hair, a straight nose and a thin line of blood beneath one ear. His face looked almost peaceful. The mouth moved without expression as the Brute stepped over the collapsed concrete.
“Brute confirmed,” Sera said. “Front armor heavy.”
Andrew's threat display changed color.
The creature did not turn toward the nearest mech.
It turned toward the workshop yard.
Toward the vans.
“Juno, main cannon?” Andrew asked.
“Can penetrate if I get a clear side angle,” Juno replied. “But the vans are behind it right now.”
“Hold fire. Darius, keep those people covered.”
“Understood.”
The Brute began moving down the road.
Each step sent water out from the drainage ditch. It was slower than the XR-17s, but it had enough mass to tear apart the workshop buildings if it reached them.
Mara brought up the field west of the road.
“Hard ground there,” she said. “We can draw it out. Clear line away from the vans.”
Andrew checked the distance.

He could race past the Brute, pursue the smaller Reclaimed toward the north and perhaps find their entry route. The open fields offered him speed and room to fight. It was tempting to turn this into a hunt.
Behind him, Leonie's vans were still parked beside Darius.
“Your field,” Andrew told Mara. “I'll draw it west. You keep the road covered.”
“Good. Don't pull it beyond the next rise. We lose sight of you there.”
“Understood.”
Andrew pushed his XR-17 across the workshop lane and into the open field.
The machine accelerated hard, its body remaining low as its six legs caught the firm ground. He cut north, turned the turret and fired his rotary cannon into the Brute's armored shoulder.
The rounds struck but failed to slow it.
The human head turned toward him.
Andrew fired again.
The Brute changed course.
“It's following,” Sera confirmed.
“That's the idea.”
The creature charged into the field, digging deep tracks in the wet ground. Andrew shifted sideways and let it pass, then fired into its upper torso from behind.
It turned with startling balance. A heavy arm swept toward his canopy.
Andrew dropped his mech low and lunged beneath the swing. The limb passed overhead but clipped an outer plate, jolting him against the harness.
His alarms sounded.
“Andrew, damage?” Yelena asked.
“Outer armor. No joint warnings.”
“Stay out of its arms.”
“Working on it.”
The Brute faced him again.

Along the road, Mara held her position while Sera and Darius destroyed the remaining Huskframes trying to reach the vans. Nico had restored a short-range link to west watch and was relaying the field's friendly positions.
“West watch confirms no civilian traffic beyond the rise,” Nico reported. “Firing lane clear if the Brute stays west.”
Juno advanced to the field entrance, turret following the creature.
“I have a line,” he said. “Need it another twenty meters out.”
Andrew looked at the Brute, then at the terrain ahead. He could have pulled it much farther away, but that would leave the escort with one less mech and no direct line of sight to him.
“Mara, enough room?” he asked.
“Another fifteen meters. Then turn it toward you.”
Andrew followed her instruction.
The Brute came again. He waited until it committed to the charge, then drove sideways. His XR-17 covered the distance in a single smooth burst. The six legs kept the low body level through the turn.
The creature missed.
“Juno,” Andrew said. “You have your angle.”
“Charging.”
Andrew saw the orange channel of Juno's main cannon brighten against the gray field.
“Firing.”
The discharge struck beneath the Brute's shoulder. The force drove its massive torso sideways, buckling armor and exposing a cavity of cables and pale tissue.
The creature dropped to one knee.
It began to rise.
“Still moving,” Sera said.
“Cannon cooling,” Juno replied.
Andrew rotated his turret toward the opening Juno had made.
The human head above the cavity remained intact. Its lips moved once, as though trying to tell him something.
Andrew checked the line behind it. Empty field. No vehicles. No friendly positions.
“All units, clear of the western firing line?”
Mara answered first. Then Akari, Darius, Sera, Yelena and Nico. Juno confirmed his mech was out of the shot.
Andrew fired.

The energy discharge drove into the Brute's exposed structure. Its arms locked in place, then fell loose. The torso collapsed, the enormous body hitting the ground hard enough to shake the workshop windows.
Andrew kept his turret on it.
The head was still visible above the twisted armor. For a moment it faced the sky, eyes open.
Then the wreckage settled over it.
“Brute down,” Andrew said.
“Two Huskframes at the road,” Mara replied. “Don't advance.”
Darius's rotary cannon sounded behind him.
“Handled,” Darius said.
Andrew waited for movement.
None came.
“Status,” he ordered. “Everyone, report.”
“Mara, functional.”
“Darius, functional.”
“Juno, functional. Cannon hot but intact.”
“Akari, functional.”
“Sera, functional. Right sensor array needs cleaning.”
“Yelena, functional. Checking the technicians.”
“Nico, functional. Local radio restored.”
Andrew breathed out. “Andrew, functional.”
Eight voices, including his own.
A shout came from the workshop yard.
“Medic!”
Yelena was already out of her cockpit when Andrew arrived.
The second van's passenger door stood open. Mika sat on the pavement with blood darkening one sleeve. A piece of glass had cut his forearm when the Crawler struck the van.
“It's just a scratch,” Mika was saying.
“Good,” Yelena replied. “Then this won't take long.”
She cleaned the wound, checked the movement in his fingers and wrapped the arm while Leonie held his shoulder.
“You've done this before,” Mika said.
Yelena did not look up. “Yes.”
“How many times?”
“Enough to know you should hold still.”
Mika held still.
Andrew climbed down beside Juno's mech. Juno was already checking the repaired bearing, fingers tracing the retaining collar.
“Anything loose?” Andrew asked.
“No. She handled that charge beautifully.” Juno crouched to inspect a scored side plate. “That Stalker got close, though.”
“You still happy with yesterday's repair?”
“More than ever.”
Juno stood and looked toward the fallen Brute.
For a moment he said nothing.
“Never like seeing the faces,” he said at last.
Andrew followed his gaze.

A Huskframe lay near the road with its coat twisted beneath its body. The face was still that of an ordinary person, except for the motionless eyes and the metal structure visible where its collar should have been.
“No,” Andrew agreed.
Darius approached carrying a water bottle and the parcel of food he'd saved from breakfast.
“Anybody hungry?” he asked.
Leonie looked at him as if she'd misheard.
“Now?”
“Especially now,” Darius said.
Nico appeared at his shoulder. “He considers this a medical necessity.”
“That's because you complain if I don't feed you,” Darius replied.
“It's the only way to make myself heard.”
Mika laughed. The sound came out in a surprised burst, and he looked embarrassed by it.
Yelena tied off the bandage. “There. You're allowed to laugh. You're not allowed to lift anything heavy.”
“That's most of my job,” Mika said.
“Then you'll supervise.”
Leonie took a roll from Darius. “He'll love that.”
Andrew checked the road. Broken concrete partly blocked the culvert, but there was enough space for the vans to move through one at a time.
“Akari, Sera, sweep the approaches,” he said. “Nico, get the relay on local radio. Mara, check the safest way through. We don't move until everyone confirms.”
The reports came back clear.
The vans pulled out of the hardstand.
The last stretch to the relay took less than ten minutes.

The station stood on a low ridge behind a bent fence, with two squat aerial towers and a concrete equipment building between them. The exterior looked as if it had survived several storms and at least one careless artillery crew.
Nico studied it through his cockpit display.
“We fought all that way for this?”
Leonie was getting out of her van. “You want pretty architecture, find a museum.”
Juno laughed.
Inside the equipment building, the air smelled of damp insulation and hot plastic. Several warning lights flashed on a cabinet beside the primary transmitter.
Leonie opened the housing and stared.
“Well,” she said.
Andrew waited. “Good well or bad well?”
“Both.”
Brown water had seeped into the lower coupling box. A cracked connector sat beneath a tangle of corroded contacts. The backup power feed entered through the same compartment.
“There's your problem,” Leonie said. “Storm water ruined the coupling. The backup's been carrying the load through half a connection.”
“Can you replace it?” Andrew asked.
“Yes. That's why I brought a spare.”
She turned to Mika. “Dry housing, insulated connectors, portable test set. Carefully. And let Oskar carry the battery.”
Mika gave Yelena a wary glance before obeying.
Andrew left the technicians to their work and returned to his mech.

The squad spread around the station, covering the northern approach, the culvert road and the fields beyond the ridge. Their main cannons cooled while the smaller weapons remained ready. In the distance, artillery continued to fire.
Andrew watched the route on his screen.

One section of the communications network had failed, and civilian movement across several checkpoints had stopped with it. It wasn't the greatest threat facing Germany. It might not even make the evening briefing.
But it mattered to the people waiting for someone to tell them they could go home.
“Andrew,” Mara said on their private channel.
“Go ahead.”
“Your armor report came through. Left plate has a shallow fracture.”
“Juno saw it.”
“He says he can repair it.”
“Then we'll have something for him to do when we get back.”
Mara paused. “You should have told me when that Brute clipped you.”
“I said I was still moving.”
“That wasn't what I asked.”
He looked at her friendly marker on the map.
“I didn't lose control,” Andrew said. “I had no joint warnings.”
“I know. I saw the telemetry.”
“Then why ask?”
“Because I'm allowed to worry about you, ja?”
Andrew smiled faintly. “Noted.”
“Good.”
The private channel closed.
Inside the relay station, metal tools clicked against the cabinet. Leonie gave brisk instructions. Mika called out voltage readings, corrected one, then reported a steady result.
Nico had patched a short-range set into the relay's test circuit.
“Local link is good,” he said. “Long-range still dead.”
“Give me five minutes,” Leonie replied.
“You said five minutes ten minutes ago.”
“Would twenty make you happier?”
“Five is excellent.”
A soft electronic tone sounded in Andrew's cockpit.
Then another.
The northern observation markers, which had been uncertain all morning, began appearing on the map.
“Nico?” Andrew asked.
“Wait,” Nico said. “I think I have it.”
Static washed across the channel.
A faint voice emerged.
“...relay three... anybody receiving...?”
Nico sat forward. “Convoy control, this is Relay Three. Receiving. Stand by for verification.”
The reply was stronger.
“Relay Three, identify.”
Leonie read out the authentication sequence. Nico repeated the challenge response and waited for confirmation.
A clear tone sounded.
“Primary link stable,” he said. “Checking backup.”
Leonie's voice trembled with fatigue and relief. “Backup stable too.”
Andrew checked the time. The repair had taken longer than the technicians hoped, but the medical convoy still had time to make its scheduled passage.
“Contact the roadblock,” he told Nico.
“Already doing it.”
A new voice came onto the channel. “Southern convoy gate, go ahead.”
“Walker escort at Relay Three,” Nico said. “Communications restored. Local approach secured. Official release confirmation should follow.”
A brief pause.
Then the voice answered, “You have no idea how good it is to hear you.”
Nico grinned at his display.
“I have some idea.”
Leonie came outside with her gloves tucked beneath one arm. For the first time since meeting her, Andrew saw her relax.
“Final diagnostics look good,” she said. “It's working.”
“Properly working?” Andrew asked.
“Don't ruin this for me.”
“Wouldn't dream of it.”
The first convoy cleared its roadblock a few minutes later.
The medical convoy reported that it had received the restored route information and was preparing to move. The workers at the depot confirmed that their local telephone link had returned.
“That's two,” Nico announced.
“Three,” Sera corrected.
“What?”
“Maintenance truck at the western checkpoint. They were waiting too.”
Nico nodded solemnly. “Three convoys. An impressive achievement by the handsome communications officer.”
“Leonie fixed the transmitter,” Sera said.
“I supervised emotionally.”
Leonie heard him. “I'll accept joint credit.”
Darius approached carrying one of the last breakfast parcels.
“Leonie,” he said, “have you eaten anything since we left the depot?”
She stared at the roll.
“No.”
“Then this is yours.”
She accepted it carefully, as if it were some complicated piece of equipment.
“Thank you,” she said.
At the edge of the yard, Akari approached the three technicians with her camera.
“Would you mind a picture?” she asked.
Mika glanced at his bandaged arm. “Like this?”
“Exactly like that,” Akari said. “You did the job. You should have proof.”
Leonie looked at the ruined station behind her.
“Do we have to stand in front of the building?”
“Only if you want to.”
“Good. Because it's hideous.”
Akari laughed and gathered them beside the vans.
Andrew watched her fuss over their positions, asking Oskar to step closer and Mika to turn his injured arm away from the lens. When she reached the camera timer, she stopped.
“Actually,” she said, “would someone else take it? I'd like to be in this one.”
Nico looked at her.
“Oh, no,” he said.
“Oh, yes,” Akari replied.
Andrew took the camera before the argument could become complicated.
“Everybody stand still,” he said.
Akari joined the technicians, smiling broadly. Leonie looked exhausted. Mika kept glancing at the bandage. Oskar stood very straight, hands at his sides.
The camera clicked.
Akari hurried over to inspect the picture.
“Perfect,” she said.
“You're getting easier to please,” Andrew replied.
“Don't be ridiculous. I still have standards.”
He was about to answer when the restored northern communications channel filled with new traffic.
A battery requested updated coordinates.
A position farther north reported contact beyond its forward obstacles.
Another officer asked for reinforcements at a road junction.
The voices were tired and matter-of-fact. They weren't announcing a victory or a catastrophe. They were trying to keep people informed enough to get through the next hour.
Mara came onto the squad channel. “Depot confirms we're clear to return after the technicians finish packing. No new orders yet.”
“Understood,” Andrew said.
He looked at the eight friendly markers on his display.
“Everyone holds until Leonie's team is ready,” he ordered. “Then we go home together.”
“Can we go faster on the return?” Juno asked.
“If the corridor's clear,” Andrew replied.
“Beautiful.”
“And don't start racing Nico.”
Nico sounded offended. “Why am I being blamed for a race that hasn't happened?”
“Experience,” Sera said.
Akari lifted her camera again.
“Andrew! One more, before we leave.”
“Of what?”
“All of us. With the technicians.”
Mara sighed over the radio. “You already have one.”
“That was a picture of them.”
“And this one?”
“Proof that we were here.”
Andrew looked at the technicians, the restored aerials and his friends waiting beside their mechs. Then he checked the road and the perimeter one last time.
“All right,” he said. “One picture.”
Akari smiled. “Ten seconds.”
“That's what you said yesterday,” Nico replied.
Andrew laughed.
For once, they had time.
